papers.title: The Bern Sleep-Wake Registry: A 25-year multimodal resource for data-driven sleep medicine
papers.abstract: Background: Sleep-wake-circadian disorders are prevalent and contribute substantially to morbidity, mortality and reduced quality of life. Evaluation in real-world settings is essential to capture their complexity and association with long-term outcomes. Most sleep-wake registries are restricted to selected populations, lack systematic integration of objective sleep-wake-circadian assessments with the clinical data and provide limited follow-up. To address these limitations, we established the Bern Sleep-Wake Registry based on real-world data from a tertiary University Hospital sleep center. Methods: The registry includes data from patients referred to the multidisciplinary Sleep- Center at Inselspital, University Hospital Bern (funded in 1990), from the year 2000 onwards who underwent at least one objective assessment such as polysomnography, daytime sleep-wake recordings, vigilance tests, and actigraphy. The registry integrates clinical information, questionnaire scores, outputs of objective assessments and raw signal data, and is regularly updated to incorporate new patients and longitudinal follow-up information. Results: As of September 2025, records from over 11000 patients were evaluated (median age: 50 years (interquantile range 36, 61); 65% male). The most common sleep-wake-circadian disorders were sleep-related breathing disorders (67%), insomnia disorders (15%) and central disorders of hypersomnolence (9%). Available assessments included more than 12000 polysomnographies, 2400 multiple sleep latency tests, 2100 maintenance of wakefulness tests, 1800 vigilance tests and 4500 actigraphies. Conclusions: By longitudinally integrating multimodal deep clinical phenotyping with objective assessments and raw physiological signals, the Bern Sleep-Wake Registry provides a foundation for investigating disease trajectories, identifying novel biomarkers and developing data-driven approaches to precise diagnosis, prognosis and individualized treatment.

papers.title: Digital wellbeing in the social media era: dual pathway analysis of emotional and behavioural distress indicators and public health utility
papers.abstract: Social media language and digital lifestyle behaviours are promoted as scalable signals of population mental health, but predictive models are often evaluated in ways that overstate accuracy. We analysed 20,000 tweets from 72 users, labelled by whether the account belonged to a user identified as depressed, and two synthetic datasets (100,000 and 30,000 records) linking screen time, sleep and social media use with self-reported stress. Under a conventional tweet-level split, a term-weighted logistic regression appeared accurate (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.835), but when whole users were held out its performance fell to near chance (0.595; 95% confidence interval 0.505 to 0.686), because the model largely recognised users and their topics. Depression-associated tweets were more often negative (31.7% versus 24.2%), yet sentiment alone could not identify unseen users (0.539). The two behavioural datasets gave opposite answers: strong discrimination in one (0.926), driven by short sleep, and chance in the other (0.506), so synthetic results reflect how the data were generated. At a population prevalence of 10%, positive predictive values would be 0.10 to 0.30. Digital distress signals should be validated across individuals, on real linked data and at realistic prevalence before informing public health surveillance or prevention.

papers.title: A Multi-Domain EEG Framework Integrating Spectral, Functional Connectivity, and Topological Features for Subject-Level ADHD Classification
papers.abstract: Background: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that significantly affect cognitive, academic, and social functioning. Although electroencephalography (EEG) has emerged as a promising non-invasive tool for identifying objective neurophysiological biomarkers of ADHD because of its high temporal resolution and cost-effectiveness, many existing machine learning studies rely on single-domain EEG features, which may not adequately capture the complex functional organization of the brain. Methods: This study proposes a subject-level EEG classification framework that integrates three complementary feature domains: spectral characteristics, weighted Phase Lag Index (wPLI)-based functional connectivity, and topological descriptors derived from persistent homology. EEG recordings from 121 subjects were preprocessed and segmented into overlapping windows for feature extraction. Window-level features were aggregated to generate subject-level representations. Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) was employed to select the 110 most informative features from an initial set of 1,043 descriptors. Five machine learning classifiers, including Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), were evaluated using stratified five-fold cross-validation. An ablation study was further conducted to assess the contribution of each feature domain. Model interpretability was investigated using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), two widely adopted Explainable Artificial Intelligence techniques for interpreting machine learning models. Results: Among the evaluated classifiers, the SVM achieved the highest classification performance, yielding an accuracy of 80.17%, an F1-score of 80.95%, a balanced accuracy of 80.14%, a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 86.72%, and a precision recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) of 87.34%. The ablation study demonstrated that combining spectral, functional connectivity, and topological features consistently outperformed individual feature domains, highlighting the complementary nature of these representations. Explainable AI analyses further identified functional connectivity features as the primary contributors to classification performance while confirming the additional value of spectral and topological descriptors. Conclusions: The proposed framework demonstrates that integrating spectral analysis, functional connectivity, and topological data analysis provides an effective and interpretable approach for subject-level ADHD classification from EEG recordings. The combination of recursive feature selection, multi-domain feature fusion, ablation analysis, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence establishes a transparent and reproducible pipeline that may facilitate the development of reliable EEG-based clinical decision-support systems for ADHD.

papers.title: Predictors of malaria prevention practices among HIV-positive patients attending an antiretroviral therapy clinic in Kampala, Uganda: a cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Background Malaria and HIV remain major causes of illness in sub-Saharan Africa, accounting for 94% of the global malaria burden and over two-thirds of the global HIV burden. HIV-related immunosuppression increases susceptibility to malaria, with a higher malaria burden of up to 47% and severe malaria complications compared to HIV-negative individuals. Socio-demographic factors, individual knowledge, attitude, and perception are recognized determinants of malaria prevention behaviours, but no study has modelled their combined contribution, and there is scant research on these factors among people living with HIV. We assessed the level of knowledge, attitudes, and perceptions towards malaria, and identified the predictors of malaria prevention practice among HIV-positive individuals in Kampala, Uganda. Methods This cross-sectional study enrolled 620 HIV-positive patients attending the ART clinic of China-Uganda Friendship Hospital, Naguru, selected by systematic random sampling. Data collection was conducted from 21st July 2025 to 18th August 2025 using a structured, interviewer-administered questionnaire that measured socio-demographic characteristics, knowledge, attitude, perception, and the practice of malaria prevention. Associations were assessed using Mann-Whitney U, Kruskal-Wallis H, and Spearman correlation. The independent predictors of good malaria prevention practice were identified using binary logistic regression. Results Participants had a mean age of 34.8 years, were predominantly female (68.9%), Baganda (38.1%) by tribe, and the majority had a secondary level of education(46.0%). Most had good knowledge of malaria (97.3%) and a positive attitude (90.5%), while 57.3% held a positive perception of malaria risk and prevention; only 62.6% reported good malaria prevention practice, and most prevention methods used were sleeping under a mosquito net (71.1 3%) and closing windows early in the evening (70.3%). In regression analysis, knowledge (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] 1.198, 95% CI 1.03-1.40, p = 0.023) and attitude (AOR 1.101, 95% CI 1.04-1.17, p = 0.001) independently predicted good practice, while perception did not (AOR 1.00, 95% CI 0.96-1.04, p = 0.994). Scores of Attitude, perception, and malaria prevention practices varied significantly, though non-linearly, by education level, and were highest among non-educated participants. Conclusions Despite near-universal knowledge and predominantly positive attitudes in this study, more than a third of HIV-positive participants did not practice adequate malaria prevention, and perception did not independently predict malaria prevention practice once knowledge and attitude were accounted for. Programmes seeking to close this know-do gap should pair health education with structural support for prevention tools rather than education alone.

papers.title: Daylight Saving Time, Acute Sleep Disruption, and Return-to-Baseline Patterns in All of Us Fitbit Data
papers.abstract: Seasonal daylight saving time (DST) transitions abruptly alter the alignment between clock time, environmental light, and sleep. In preregistered analyses, we used longitudinal Fitbit data from the All of Us Research Program to compare sleep around 13 seasonal transitions in Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah with sleep on the same dates in Arizona, where clocks do not change. The sample included 1,522 participants and 6,658 participant-transition windows. Following the spring transition, sleep duration changed more from one night to the next in Mountain states than in Arizona (14.6 minutes, 95% CI [7.2, 22.0]), even though sleep duration itself on day +1 showed little evidence of a DST-related reduction (-8.4 minutes, 95% CI [-17.3, 0.6]). Sleep timing shifted later after the spring transition and about 28 minutes earlier after the fall transition. Among Mountain-state observations with a large post-transition departure from usual sleep duration, the median return to the usual range was two nights. Nearly the same two-night pattern appeared in Arizona after similarly large sleep departures, indicating that this return pattern was not specific to DST. Greater baseline sleep-duration variability predicted a greater likelihood of remaining outside the usual range at days +7 and +14. Seasonal clock changes produced acute sleep disruption, while the Arizona comparison shows that a rapid return to baseline should not be interpreted as the duration of recovery from DST itself.

papers.title: A Novel Digital Phenotype of Physical Activity: Associations with Heart Rate Fragmentation
papers.abstract: Background Heart rate fragmentation (HRF) has emerged as a novel marker of sinoatrial instability and neuroautonomic dysregulation and is a predictor of incident cardiovascular disease (CVD) events and cardiovascular mortality. Leveraging heart rate fragmentation as a novel measure may help us better understand the prognostic significance of physical activity. Physical activity (PA) patterns are multidimensional and difficult to study holistically, however. We sought to examine for novel PA clusters in a cohort of veteran men and evaluate their prognostic significance based on their associations with neuroautonomic dysregulation. Methods In this cross-sectional study, we examined 602 male veterans from the Vietnam Era Twins Study of Electrophysiology in Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (VETS-EP) who were enrolled between 2022 and 2026. Accelerometry data were used to derive physical activity parameters across 6 domains: volume, sedentary behavior, intensity, diurnal pattern, fragmentation, and variability. Heart rate fragmentation was assessed using percentage of inflection points (PIP), inverse average length of segments (IALS), percentage of short segments (PSS), and percentage of alternating segments (PAS). Gaussian mixture models were used to derive digital phenotypes of physical activity, and associations with heart rate fragmentation were assessed using linear mixed models. Results Participants had a mean age of 73.8 {+/-} 2.9 years and 93.2% reported White race. Two overlapping phenotypes of physical activity patterns were identified: a compact-early phenotype, characterized by earlier activity timing and slightly greater overall activity, and a diffuse-late phenotype, characterized by later activity timing and greater heterogeneity in activity volume. In fully adjusted models, the diffuse-late phenotype was associated with higher PIP, the primary outcome ({beta}: 1.199, 95% CI: 0.034 to 2.363, p-value: 0.044), and higher IALS ({beta}: 0.01210, 95% CI: 0.00048 to 0.02373, p-value: 0.041), but not PSS or PAS, compared with the compact-early phenotype. Conclusions In older male veterans, Gaussian mixture model phenotyping identified two overlapping physical activity phenotypes, differing mainly in diurnal timing and in the dispersion of overall activity, that were associated with modest differences in heart rate fragmentation. These phenotypes provide a framework for capturing complex physical activity patterns. Future prospective studies representing diverse populations are needed to validate such phenotypes.

papers.title: Parsing the Pediatric Mood Spectrum in U.S. Youth: Transdiagnostic Severity Versus Phenotypic Specificity
papers.abstract: Objective: Emotion dysregulation and irritability occur across pediatric disorders, complicating distinctions between general symptom burden and specific clinical presentations. Person-centered analyses can look at profiles of scores to identify groups with similar presentations. We examined whether modeling shared and domain-specific symptom variance identified differentiated profiles in youth. Method: Caregivers of 2,187 US youth ages 6-18 completed 87 items assessing emotion dysregulation, depression, mania-related symptoms, sleep-related impairment, and attention and behavioral problems. An ordinal bifactor model estimated one general and 13 specific factors. Latent profile analyses used standardized scores on all 14 factors, with an expanded raw-score analysis as a comparator. We examined caregiver-reported diagnoses and functioning and approximately two-week classification agreement among 166 recontacted caregivers. Results: The general factor accounted for 62% of common variance ({omega}H=.94), although model fit was mixed (CFI=.884; RMSEA=.058; SRMR=.092). A provisional four-class solution distinguished population-modal (67.4%), internalizing (11.8%), attention/hyperactivity (11.0%), and unusual-thought/elevated-mood (9.8%) profiles. Entropy was .83, but model enumeration and initialization checks did not establish a unique solution. Profiles showed overlapping diagnostic and functional correlates. Recontact agreement was 78.9% ({kappa}=.60). Irritability-specific reliability was limited, constraining interpretation of its weak profile differentiation. Conclusions: General symptom burden coexisted with differentiated residual symptom patterns. These findings support evaluating severity alongside symptom configuration, without equating profiles with diagnoses or weak residual irritability signals with limited clinical relevance. Measurement refinement, model-selection verification, and confirmation of classification-error-adjusted associations are needed before clinical application, but profiles could simplify clinical interpretation of sets of scales.

papers.title: Real-time wearable detection of respiratory infections in pediatric transplant households
papers.abstract: Consumer-grade wearables can continuously and longitudinally measure health signals such as heart rate (HR), activity, and sleep. While changes in these signals have been implicated in the early detection of infection (e.g., influenza, SARS-CoV-2) and real-time alerting systems have been developed, evidence from prospective deployment in pediatric transplant households remains limited. Here, we study the application of a resting heart rate (RHR)-based real-time alerting algorithm to detect respiratory virus infection in a cohort of solid organ transplant recipients and their household members (n=146) in a Phase IV clinical trial (NCT06161454). Reliable and efficient alerting for infection events may be particularly relevant for this population, enabling isolation, clinical management, and/or treatment. Of 31 antigen-test outcomes, nearly all (29/31, 93.5%) correspond to either influenza, COVID, or other patient-reported symptoms. We describe RHR, HR, activity, and sleep/circadian rhythm features around clinical alarm events, identifying candidate features for further investigation and algorithm improvement.

papers.title: Attenuated alpha state transitions and disrupted repetition-dependent temporal adaptation in mild cognitive impairment
papers.abstract: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) may involve impaired dynamic regulation of brain states that is not captured by conventional resting-state electroencephalography (EEG). We quantified occipital alpha (8-12 Hz) transitions during three repeated eye-opening/eye-closure cycles in 60 healthy controls (HC) and 77 participants with MCI. Eye-state events were refined from frontal ocular artifacts. Transition magnitude was measured by the log-transformed post-/pre-event energy ratio, and transition success by the expected direction of alpha change. For canonical transitions meeting prespecified fit-quality criteria, mono-exponential fitting yielded transition onset (t_onset) and the post-onset time constant (tau). MCI showed weaker alpha suppression during eye opening, weaker alpha enhancement during eye closure, and lower odds of transition success. No significant group difference in tau was detected within the canonical quality-controlled subset. In contrast, t_onset showed significant Group x Trial interactions in both conditions: HC developed later onset during eye opening and earlier onset during eye closure across repetitions, whereas MCI showed no comparable change. These findings suggest reduced alpha state-transition capacity and altered repetition-dependent temporal organization in MCI.

papers.title: Longitudinal Pain Profiles and Their Clinical and Genetic Correlates in 624,996 U.S. Veterans
papers.abstract: Importance: Pain varies in its intensity and course, yet much of our understanding of pain is based on cross-sectional assessments or longitudinal studies of selected clinical populations. Routinely collected electronic health record data may enable characterization of longitudinal pain patterns at scale. Objective: To identify longitudinal pain profiles among U.S. Veterans and characterize their clinical and polygenic correlates. Design: Cohort study using electronic health record and genomic data from the Million Veteran Program, with up to 16 years of pain assessments collected between 2000 to 2025. Setting: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs health care system. Participants: Million Veteran Program participants assigned to African-like, Admixed American-like, East Asian-like, European-like, or South Asian-like genetically inferred ancestry groups who have at least three years of outpatient numeric rating scale pain records. Exposures: Outpatient pain ratings and polygenic scores for psychiatric, sleep, and substance use traits. Main Outcomes and Measures: Pain profiles were identified using Gaussian finite mixture modeling of pain intensity, directional change, and within-person variability. Profiles were characterized by pain, psychiatric and substance use diagnoses, opioid exposure, body mass index, and polygenic scores. Results: Among 624,996 participants (Mean [SD] age at first pain rating=53.4 [13.5] years; 568,833 [91.0%] male), 51,731,567 outpatient pain ratings were analyzed. Three profiles were identified: stable no pain, stable mild pain, and mild-to-moderate increasing pain. Compared with the stable no pain profile, the increasing pain profile had higher odds of chronic pain (OR=21.14 [95% CI: 18.96-23.57]), opioid use disorder (OR=9.32 [95% CI: 8.31-10.45]), opioid exposure (OR=8.61 [95% CI: 8.41-8.83]), major depressive disorder (OR=3.77 [95% CI: 3.67-3.87]), and posttraumatic stress disorder (OR=3.72 [95% CI: 3.61-3.84]). Associations were attenuated but remained after adjustment for mean pain severity. Polygenic scores for depression, insomnia, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, and tobacco use disorder were the most consistent predictors of increasing pain across the three largest genetically inferred ancestry groups. Conclusions and Relevance: Longitudinal modeling of routinely collected pain scores identified pain profiles associated with clinical burden and polygenic liability. These profiles captured clinically meaningful information beyond mean pain severity alone, highlighting the value of longitudinal pain phenotyping in electronic health record data.
